newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Cenbank sees intl reserves shrinking-paper.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Cenbank sees intl reserves shrinking-paper.

text.p: New import financing rules, announced earlier this year by Brazil's Central Bank, could trigger a drop in the country's foreign currency reserves of up to $8 billion, a Central Bank director said.

Central Bank Political Economy director Francisco "Chico" Lopes said in an interview published in daily Jornal do Brasil on Sunday, that authorities expect the foreign reserve levels, currently at $59 billion, to drop by around $5 billion.
"Some studies show that could be as much as $8 billion," Lopes told the newspaper.
Lopes said the new rules, which were announced in late March, included restrictions to import financing and were designed to help make Brazilian-made products more competitive.
He said the drop in reserves would be compensated by a smaller trade deficit.
"We are prepared over the next 12 months to see a small drop in reserves," Lopes said.

Brazil's fast growing trade deficit, forecast to exceed $11 billion this year, is seen by many as the most worrying element of the country's three year-old anti-inflation plan. Brazil last year posted a trade deficit of $5.54 billion.
Lopes said Brazil had a "comfortable" level of foreign reserves. "We don't feel it is important to increase the volume of reserves. We have space to lose a few," he said.
Lopes said he hoped Brazil would introduce a more flexible foreign exchange management mechanism within a period of three to four years.
He said that to allow the real currency to float freely, without any Central Bank intervention would be premature. "We need more time to build confidence in our stabilization process."

The Central Bank currently "manages" the real foreign exchange market by determining preset trading "bands" and calling currency tenders which it uses to signal the level at which it considers the currency should be trading.

"We would like to give more flexibility to our foreign exchange mechanism at a time when confidence is such that, when we introduce that greater flexibility, that should not trigger no speculative devaluation movement," he said.
